syllabus_version.title: CBSE Curriculum for the Academic Year 2026-27

topics.title: Square numbers and the locker puzzle

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why only square numbers have an odd number of factors, using partner factors.
Recognise a square number as a number multiplied by itself and as the area of a square.

topics.title: Patterns and properties of perfect squares

concepts.learning_objective: Use the units digit to decide when a number cannot be a perfect square.
Relate the trailing zeros and the parity of a number to those of its square.

topics.title: Perfect squares, odd numbers and triangular numbers

concepts.learning_objective: Use the fact that the sum of the first n odd numbers is n squared.
Count the numbers lying between two consecutive perfect squares.
Recognise that two consecutive triangular numbers add up to a square.
State the square roots of a perfect square and find the side of a square from its area.
Use prime factorisation to test for perfect squares and find square roots.
Estimate the square root of a number lying between two perfect squares.
Recognise a perfect cube as a number multiplied by itself three times.
Evaluate statements about the units digits, parity, zeros and digit counts of cubes.
Use taxicab numbers and the odd-number pattern for cubes.

topics.title: Cube roots, successive differences and history

concepts.learning_objective: Find cube roots and make numbers perfect cubes using prime factorisation.
Compute successive differences of squares and cubes and interpret the pattern.
Recall the Babylonian and ancient Indian terms for squares, cubes and roots.

topics.title: Experiencing the Power Play: folding paper

concepts.learning_objective: Calculate the thickness of a sheet of paper after a given number of folds when each fold doubles it.
Explain how repeated doubling makes a quantity grow by the same factor over equal numbers of steps.

topics.title: Exponential notation: base, exponent and prime factors

concepts.learning_objective: Identify the base and exponent and write repeated products in exponential form.
Express a number as a product of powers of its prime factors.
Decide the sign and value of powers of negative numbers.

topics.title: Operations with exponents and counting combinations

concepts.learning_objective: Use the rules n^a x n^b = n^(a+b) and (n^a)^b = n^(ab) to simplify expressions.
Use m^a x n^a = (mn)^a to combine powers with the same exponent.
Count combinations and passwords by multiplying the number of choices at each step.

topics.title: The other side of powers: division, zero and negative exponents

concepts.learning_objective: Use n^a / n^b = n^(a-b) to divide powers with the same base.
Explain why n^0 = 1 for any non-zero n.
Interpret n^(-a) as 1/n^a and simplify expressions and power lines with negative exponents.
Write numbers, including decimals, in expanded form using powers of 10.
Express large numbers in the standard form x x 10^y with 1 <= x < 10.
Compare quantities written in scientific notation using the exponent first.

topics.title: Did you ever wonder? Estimation, linear and exponential growth

concepts.learning_objective: Estimate quantities by describing relationships and making reasonable assumptions.
Distinguish additive (linear) growth from multiplicative (exponential) growth.

topics.title: Getting a sense for large numbers and a pinch of history

concepts.learning_objective: Relate lakh, crore, arab and kharab to million, billion and trillion as powers of 10.
Compare large real-world quantities by dividing numbers written in scientific notation.
Describe how Indian texts named large powers of ten and the pattern behind the names.
Recall the Indian origin of number names based on powers of 10 and of writing numbers with ten digits including 0.
Describe how the Indian numerals reached the Arab world and Europe, and why they came to be called by different names.
Use one-to-one mapping between objects and a standard sequence to count and compare collections.
Explain what a number system is and compare the strengths and limits of counting with sticks, letters and symbols.
Recall early tally-mark artefacts such as the Ishango and Lebombo bones and how tally marks represent numbers.
Interpret number systems that count in groups of a fixed size, such as the Gumulgal system of counting in twos.
Write numbers in Roman numerals by grouping them into the landmark numbers I, V, X, L, C, D and M.
Add Roman numerals by regrouping and explain why multiplication is hard in the Roman system.
Represent numbers in the Egyptian system whose landmark numbers are the powers of 10.
Find the landmark numbers of a base-n system and express numbers in it by grouping.
Explain why a system whose landmark numbers are powers of one number makes addition and multiplication easier.
Represent numbers in the Mesopotamian base-60 place value system.
Describe the place value features of the Mayan and Chinese rod numeral systems.
Explain the role of zero as a placeholder and as a number in making the Hindu system unambiguous.
Define a rectangle as a quadrilateral whose angles are all 90 degrees and recognise equivalent definitions.
Use congruence to show that the diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other, and apply this to find lengths and angles.
Distinguish a conjecture formed from measurement from a property justified by geometric deduction.
Define a square and explain why every square is a rectangle but not every rectangle is a square.
Use the facts that the diagonals of a square are equal, bisect each other at 90 degrees and bisect its angles.
Apply the result that the angles of any quadrilateral add up to 360 degrees.
Justify the angle sum of a quadrilateral by dividing it into two triangles with a diagonal.
Define a parallelogram and deduce that its adjacent angles are supplementary and its opposite angles are equal.
Use the facts that the opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal and its diagonals bisect each other.
Define a rhombus and find its angles using the facts that it is a parallelogram whose diagonals bisect its angles.
Use the facts that the diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles and bisect its angles.
Identify the quadrilateral formed when diagonals with given lengths and angle are placed so their ends can be joined.
Identify and justify the quadrilaterals formed by joining two congruent triangles along a common side.
Define a kite and use the fact that one diagonal of a kite is the perpendicular bisector of the other.
Define a trapezium and an isosceles trapezium and find unknown angles using parallel sides.
Relate rectangles, squares, parallelograms, rhombuses, kites and trapeziums using set relationships.
Explain why all expressions a ± b ± c ± d formed from the same numbers have the same parity.
Decide, using parity rules, whether an arithmetic or algebraic expression is always even.

topics.title: Pairs to make fours and Always, Sometimes, Never

concepts.learning_objective: Use the forms 4p and 4p + 2 to decide when the sum of two even numbers is a multiple of 4.
Apply the properties of divisibility of sums, multiples, factors and LCM to judge statements as always, sometimes or never true.

topics.title: What remains? Remainders in algebraic form

concepts.learning_objective: Write all numbers with a given remainder on division as an algebraic expression such as 5k + 3.
Find remainders of sums and numbers satisfying several remainder conditions without long division.
Use the remainders of place values on division by 9 to find the remainder of a number.
Apply the digit-sum tests for divisibility by 9 and 3, including finding missing digits.
Use the alternating pattern of place values to test divisibility by 11 and find the remainder.
Choose factor tests based on prime factorisation to check divisibility by numbers such as 24 and 44.
Compute the digital root of a number by repeatedly adding its digits.
Relate the digital root of a number to its remainder on division by 9.
Solve addition cryptarithms using carries and place value reasoning.
Solve multiplication cryptarithms using size limits and units-digit patterns.
State and use the distributive property a(b + c) = ab + ac and its form (a + b)c = ac + bc.
Work out how a product ab changes when one or both numbers are increased or decreased.
Expand (a + m)(b + n) and its sign variants by multiplying each term of one bracket with each term of the other.
Identify like terms and add them to simplify an expanded product.

topics.title: Fast multiplication using the distributive property

concepts.learning_objective: Multiply any number by 11 in one line by adding neighbouring digits with carries.
Use 101 = 100 + 1, 1001 = 1000 + 1 and 99 = 100 - 1 to multiply quickly.

topics.title: Square of the sum and difference of two numbers

concepts.learning_objective: Use Identity 1A, (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², to expand and to compute squares.
Use Identity 1B, (a - b)² = a² - 2ab + b², to expand and to compute squares.

topics.title: Difference of squares and investigating patterns

concepts.learning_objective: Use Identity 1C, (a + b)(a - b) = a² - b², for quick products and to express numbers as differences of squares.
Explain the pattern 2(a² + b²) = (a + b)² + (a - b)² using identities.
Compute squares quickly using a² = (a + b)(a - b) + b².

topics.title: Mind the mistake and many ways to a pattern

concepts.learning_objective: Find and correct mistakes in expanding and simplifying algebraic expressions.
Show that different expressions found for the same pattern or area simplify to the same expression.
Recognise that a figure keeps its shape when its width and height are multiplied by the same factor.
Explain why adding or subtracting the same amount to width and height distorts a figure.
Interpret a ratio a : b as 'for every a units of the first quantity there are b units of the second' and identify its terms.
Reduce a ratio to its simplest form by dividing both terms by their HCF, using the same units.
Decide whether two ratios are proportional by comparing their simplest forms or the factor of change.
Show that adding the same number to both terms of a ratio generally changes the ratio.
Use a : b :: c : d implies ad = bc to find an unknown fourth term.
Identify pramana, phala, ichchha and ichchhaphala and apply the Rule of Three.
Use the same units in both ratios and recognise situations that are not direct proportion.
Divide a quantity x in the ratio m : n into parts m x/(m + n) and n x/(m + n).
Find the new ratio, or the amount to add, when one component of a mixture is changed.
Convert units of length, area and volume before solving proportion problems.
Convert temperatures between Celsius and Fahrenheit using F = (9/5) C + 32.
